My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

The world is a dangerous place

issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together' directly conflicts with 'I can talk about what happened very easily.' For a severe mugging-related PTSD profile, markedly fragmented recall and very easy verbal access to the trauma narrative are hard to reconcile as describing the same current memory presentation.

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: The Memory node is internally incoherent for a severe mugging/robbery PTSD presentation: 'I can talk about what happened very easily' suggests low avoidance and relatively integrated, verbally accessible trauma memory, whereas simultaneously endorsing very vivid detailed recall and body-based painful reliving implies a highly sensory, distressing, poorly integrated trauma memory. This combination is possible in milder cases, but here it is hard to reconcile clinically within the same Memory profile. The Negative Appraisals items are coherent for robbery trauma, but the Memory selections do not fit cleanly with that node pattern or with the strong Negative Appraisals ↔ Memory linkage in the formulation.

issues.item: Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next
issues.explanation: This item is more characteristic of ongoing threat/safety behavior than of a pure negative appraisal. In this profile, Threat is not endorsed and all Threat-related edges are inactive, while the active formulation is specifically centered on a Memory ↔ Negative Appraisals loop. The mistrust items fit robbery-related appraisals, but 'Constant Vigilance' introduces a prominent current-threat theme that is not supported elsewhere in the profile.

vignette:
Rajesh's Vigilance

Rajesh Patel was thirty-two when he was attacked outside the parking garage of the office complex where he worked as a housekeeper. It was a Tuesday evening in October, just before seven, when the light had gone thin and the garage was nearly empty. He had finished his shift-mopping the lobby, emptying the bins from the executive floors-and was walking toward his car when a man emerged from between two vehicles. There was no warning. The man grabbed him from behind, wrenching his right arm upward with such force that Rajesh felt the shoulder socket scream. A second figure appeared, and in the confusion of movement and pain, Rajesh's face was slammed against the concrete pillar. His left cheekbone took the impact. The attackers wanted his wallet, his phone, his watch. The whole thing lasted perhaps ninety seconds. They ran. Rajesh sat on the cold garage floor, bleeding from his cheekbone, his shoulder throbbing in a way that made him nauseated.

The physical injuries healed within weeks. His cheekbone was badly bruised but not fractured. His shoulder remained tender, stiff, but he regained most of its range of motion. What did not heal was the clarity with which he could see it all happening again. When the memory surfaced-and it surfaced often, without warning-Rajesh could feel the exact pressure of the man's grip on his arm, the specific burning sensation as his face scraped against the concrete. His left cheekbone would ache in sympathy with the memory, and his right shoulder would tighten as if the hand were still there, still pulling. These sensations were so vivid and so localized that Rajesh sometimes found himself touching his face or rolling his shoulder, checking that nothing was actually happening in that moment.

What made it worse was that he could not explain it to anyone. His wife, Priya, had asked him repeatedly in those first weeks what had happened, wanting the details, wanting to understand. But when Rajesh tried to describe it, the words scattered. He knew the sequence of events-he could see them perfectly in his mind-but the moment he opened his mouth, he found himself unable to construct the narrative. He would start to speak and then stop, frustrated and ashamed. Eventually he gave her the bare facts: he had been robbed, he was fine, it was over. She accepted this, but he could see the worry in her eyes, the sense that something larger was being left unsaid.

In the months that followed, Rajesh's relationship to the world shifted in ways that felt both involuntary and absolutely rational. He had come to believe that people were fundamentally not what they appeared to be. The man who had attacked him had given no sign beforehand. He had simply emerged from the ordinary landscape of the parking garage as if he had always been a threat, waiting. This logic extended outward. The colleagues who greeted him cheerfully each morning-were they really friendly, or were they performing? The security guard who waved at him-how well did the man actually know him? Rajesh found himself scrutinizing faces, watching for the moment when a pleasant expression might slip and reveal something underneath. He was certain now that people could not be trusted, not because of any specific betrayal, but because the parking garage had shown him that trust was a luxury built on a foundation of willful blindness.

The world itself had become visibly dangerous in a way it had not been before. Not in the abstract sense of statistics or news reports, but in the concrete, moment-to-moment sense of walking through space. Rajesh began taking different routes to his car, avoiding the garage entirely on some evenings, parking instead in the street and walking further. He stopped going to the Indian grocery store he and Priya had frequented for years because it required walking through a parking lot. He declined invitations to go out in the evenings. Priya's concern deepened. His supervisor at the housekeeping company noticed that Rajesh was sometimes distracted, sometimes tense, and that he had begun requesting assignments that kept him on the upper floors of the building, away from the garage level.

It was Priya who finally insisted he speak to someone. She had watched him become smaller, more guarded, more isolated. She had felt the distance growing between them-the way he flinched when she touched his shoulder, the way he seemed to be listening for something just beyond the threshold of her awareness. She made the appointment herself. Now, sitting in the therapist's office, Rajesh is struggling to articulate why he came. He knows something is wrong. He knows he cannot go on like this. But what he fears most is that if he stops being vigilant, if he stops believing that the world is fundamentally dangerous and that people cannot be trusted, something terrible will happen again. The attack may have lasted ninety seconds, but its logic has become the structure through which he now interprets everything.
